claims.text: Cutlets are coated in wheat flour and panko (bread crumbs) and deep-fried, so the breading is wheat-based and the shared fryer carries gluten.
The table is set with a traditional-style soy sauce, which is wheat-based, alongside a house-made sauce typically also containing wheat.
Everything is pork-based and fried in a lard blend (Dutch lard plus house-rendered lard), so there is animal fat throughout the kitchen.

name: 手打ちそば処 くら (Teuchi Soba-dokoro Kura)

claims.text: Wheat-flour udon is made in the same kitchen and soba is typically cut with some wheat, so gluten cross-contact is likely.
Soba tsuyu / dipping sauce is based on wheat-containing soy sauce.
Broths and tsuyu use fish (katsuo) dashi; the signature bowl is duck.

name: 鮨処 あさの川 (Sushidokoro Asanogawa)

claims.text: As a traditional sushi house, dishes are served with standard (wheat-based) soy sauce and seasonings; no gluten-free soy sauce or celiac accommodation is documented.
The kitchen is entirely seafood-based (raw fish, shellfish, fish dashi), so vegan diners cannot avoid cross-contact; no plant-based menu exists.

This is a casual counter in an open-air food court where curry, hot dogs and other quick bites are served side by side. Curry sauces are usually thickened with wheat flour and hot dogs come on wheat buns, so a shared cooking and prep area like this carries a real risk of gluten cross-contact. Treat it as not safe for celiac diners unless staff can confirm a specific gluten-free preparation.

No information about the soy sauce or seasonings used here is documented. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so assume curry, sauces and toppings may include wheat-based seasoning until staff confirm otherwise.

No vegan-specific dishes or preparation details are documented for this spot, and the menu leans on curry and hot dogs. Shared equipment in a food-court setting makes cross-contact with meat and dairy likely. Vegan diners should confirm ingredients and handling directly with the counter.

This is shojin-ryori, which is fully vegetarian/vegan but NOT inherently gluten-free. Fu (wheat gluten) is a defining ingredient of Kyoto temple cuisine and appears across shojin courses, so the standard menu is not celiac-safe and a dedicated gluten-free preparation would have to be arranged in advance.

Courses are built around yuba, tofu and seasonal vegetables; while some items may be naturally wheat-free, no gluten-free protocol or allergen labeling is published, so cross-contact in a wheat-gluten kitchen should be assumed unless confirmed.

Shojin-ryori relies heavily on soy sauce and seasoned broths. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so dishes should be assumed to contain wheat-derived seasonings unless the kitchen confirms a wheat-free soy sauce is used. No source specifies a wheat-free soy sauce here.

As temple shojin-ryori, the cooking uses no animal products at all and relies on plant-based dashi (kombu/shiitake) rather than fish stock, making it well suited to vegans. This reflects the cuisine's Buddhist discipline rather than a separately certified vegan kitchen.

No published allergen-handling policy, allergy menu, or cross-contamination procedure was found. The restaurant is reservation-only and does accommodate custom arrangements by request, so allergy needs should be discussed directly when booking.
Fully vegetarian/vegan Buddhist cuisine with no animal products, light seasoning, and dishes described as gentle and easy on the stomach.
Reservation-only with the menu changing monthly and custom arrangements available by request, which gives room to communicate dietary needs ahead of the visit.

AL CAMINO presents itself as a gluten-free specialty shop, with rice-flour bread panini as the core menu and no wheat-based pizza or bread program (pizza service has ended). However, the available sources do not document its cross-contamination handling, so confirm preparation details directly before dining.

Existing dietary notes indicate the owner is gluten-free, but flag that some packaged items may share a facility. Celiac diners should verify which items are made in-house versus sourced, and ask about shared equipment.

This is an Italian deli where cheese and prosciutto feature heavily; vegan options are limited. The sources do not detail dairy-free or vegan preparation or cross-contact handling, so vegan diners should confirm specifics with staff.
The shop's listing states it can accommodate various allergies and that allergy information is available; ask staff for ingredient details on the day.
A dedicated gluten-free deli built around rice-flour bread, rather than a conventional restaurant adding a gluten-free option, which means the menu is designed without wheat from the ground up.
Rice-flour desserts (such as a rice-flour and olive-oil chocolate cake), Italian cookies, and a gluten-free Italian beer are offered, giving GF diners full-meal-plus-dessert range.

This is a Buddhist vegetarian (shojin/fucha ryori) kitchen, not a gluten-free one. Traditional shojin and fucha menus regularly include wheat gluten (fu) and soy-based items, and Japanese seasonings like soy sauce typically contain wheat, so the cuisine should not be considered celiac-safe without direct confirmation.
Vegetable tempura is a signature dish, and tempura batter is wheat-based; no source describes a separate gluten-free fryer or station, so assume shared frying oil and surfaces.

No source confirms the type of soy sauce used. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and shojin/fucha cooking relies heavily on it for seasoning, so a celiac diner should confirm directly before eating here.

The cuisine is plant-based by tradition: as Buddhist vegetarian cooking, the menu avoids meat and fish, and fucha ryori is rooted in fully meat-free Zen practice. This aligns with a vegan-friendly style, though specific accommodations are not documented.
Entirely plant-based menu in the Buddhist vegetarian tradition, so vegan diners can eat broadly across the courses.
Small, owner-run setting with private tatami rooms, which can make it easier to have a direct conversation about your dietary needs.

Some menu items are offered as gluten-free, but the kitchen also serves wheat-based dishes such as curry udon and ramen, so cross-contact with wheat is possible. There is no documented dedicated gluten-free prep area or fryer. If you have celiac disease, contact the cafe before visiting and confirm how each dish is prepared.
The curry udon and noodle dishes contain wheat and are not gluten-free.
No source confirms whether the soy sauce or seasonings used are wheat-free. As most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, celiac diners should ask staff directly which dishes use wheat-free seasoning.
The menu is primarily plant-based, but a few items contain dairy and/or eggs. Vegans should tell the staff to exclude milk and eggs from their order.

The cafe describes its food as 100% plant-based and free of the five pungent vegetables (onion, garlic, chives, leeks, shallots), though some listed items note dairy/egg use, so confirm when ordering.
The cafe states it will accommodate allergies as much as possible and invites diners to contact them in advance with dietary needs.
Staff will do their best to accommodate dietary requirements; food is prepared from scratch and cooked fresh to order, which can make custom requests easier.
A dedicated plant-based cafe near Toji Temple and Kyoto Station, with vegan, vegetarian, gluten-free, and oriental-vegetarian (no five pungent vegetables) options on the menu.
An English menu is available and the staff are described as welcoming, with dishes made fresh to order.
